en: Salutation to the illustrious Lord of Obstacles.
The Vīraśaiva Āgama.
[The First Chapter of the Vīrāgama]
The Goddess said:
"The Śaiva, Pāśupata, Vāma, and Lākula constitute the fourfold [tradition].
Among them, that which is beyond is called Śaiva; it is indeed the Śāmbhava, both gentle and fierce."

The gentle [Saumya] system is to be known as fivefold: Bhūtatantra, Gāruḍa, Vāma, Dakṣiṇa, and Siddhānta; and that which is called Nāda has emerged [from these]. Bhūtatantra is traditionally defined as that which pacifies spirits, ghosts, and the like.
The removal of the objects [of the senses] is indeed declared therein;
in that system, both the Vāma and the Dakṣiṇa Siddhāntas, Durgās are proclaimed.
The Dakṣiṇa is Śāmbhava, while the Vāma is characterized by the predominance of Śakti.
The Siddhānta is indeed pure Śaiva, as is the exclusive Śāmbhava;
the Dakṣiṇa is threefold, while the Kāmukha is the Mahāvrata.
The Śāstṛtantra and Mahāsena are divided on the right;
O Pārvatī, that which is on the left should be known as twofold: the Left and the Mixed.
The Left (Vāma) [tradition] possesses the Vāma-siddhānta, as well as the Miśra and Yāma;
it is said to consist of nine Yāmas, with the sevenfold measure as its primary element.
O you who are devoted to the vow, the threefold division of the Siddhāntas has been declared: the Vaidhānasa, the Bhāgavada, and the Pāñcarātra Śāṅkara.
Ādiśaiva, Mahāśaiva, Anādi, and Triśaivaka—
such are the divisions of Śaivism proclaimed, O Pārvatī. Another hymn has been fully described, as well as the Tantra known as Pāśupatādhika.

One should cause them to perform their respective duties according to their divisions and sub-divisions; one should arrange the sequence and the scriptures for the purpose of deluding them. When such confusion (*saṃkara*) arises among these, the king and the kingdom perish.
Therefore, the preceptor should perform everything in a manner free from confusion.
I have explained all the distinctions: confusion regarding castes (*jāti-saṅkara*), confusion regarding mantras, and indeed confusion regarding tantras.
One should avoid confusion regarding teachers, as well as confusion regarding ritual acts,
confusion regarding materials, and indeed confusion regarding sacred fires.
Thus has been declared the confusion (saṅkara) arising from the faults of the king regarding his kingdom;
likewise, there is the Vāma-miśra, the Śaiva, and the Vāma-śāmbhava.
There are countless millions of eras, as numerous as the sands of the ocean;
these include the Vāma, Pāśupata, Kālamukha, and Mahāvrata systems.
The Kāpāla-Bhairavas are Śākta; the Srāvakas are practitioners of Yoga.
There are many kinds of Śaivas, as well as Vaiṣṇavas and Pāñcarātrikas. O Umā, the Vaidhānas, Sākus, and Kaukas—these are their threefold divisions.
The Sāṅkhyas, the Carakas, the Kuṭīcakas, as well as the Haṃsas,
the Parahaṃsas, and I myself— the servant of those who speak of the Haṃsa.
O Umā, all these practitioners of the *samaya* are fond of mutual quarreling;
having abandoned all of this, they call themselves Vīraśaivas.
Īśvara said:
Excellent, excellent! You have asked a question that is most difficult to obtain—a secret of the gods, asuras, and sages, and a mystery of the mind.
O beloved, I shall explain all of that— the sequence of Vīraśaivism,
the four monasteries (maṭhas), the four liṅgas, the sixfold worship of Śambhu,
as well as conduct (ācāra), ritual action (kriyā), and the characteristics of the mudrās.
O Great Goddess, listen to all of this with a one-pointed mind.
Elsewhere: Having bowed her head to the God of gods, the Lord of the universe, who was seated upon the peak of Kailāsa, the Goddess began to hear all that [concerning] the supreme Lord,
the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction.
I wish to hear, in accordance with reality, the great truth that is the arrival of the Hero.
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, to the most excellent Vīraśaiva doctrine, which is a great secret;
I shall tell you the mystery of all the Āgamas and the Vedas.

The high-souled ones do not know the majesty of the *prāṇaliṅga*; I alone among the ends of the worlds am its knower, for it has become manifest through the Cause. In the time of the ancient Kṛta Yuga, there was a quarrel over the nectar (*sudhā*).

In this world, there was constant strife among those who were mutual enemies— the deities and the rākṣasas, the thirty gods, the asuras, and the siddhas— whose arms bristled with joy for combat. Among them were the moon, the sun, the hosts of Maruts, and other foremost siddhas and yogins.
At that time, O lady of excellent hips, the waters were intent upon the worship of the sacred seats (pīṭhas).
O Maheśvarī, in their disputes with the Rākṣasas, the gods were intent on flight; abandoning their sons, friends, kinsmen, and others, O Great Goddess.
"How can we abandon the worship of the deity received from the mouth of our own guru?"—
having reflected thus, those gods arrived, having offered their salutations.

O Great Goddess, beholding her, I spoke these words out of compassion: "O Sovereign of the Gods, why have you abandoned the worship of the deities and the worship of Śiva obtained from your guru? You are not capable of [abandoning this]; what is your purpose? Show me mercy!"
When all the gods questioned me regarding them, I spoke this which was uttered by me; then,
having repeatedly examined all the Vedas—
the Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, Atharva, and so forth— all the Vedas previously mentioned [were considered].
For their understanding, having carefully examined the secret of the divine scriptures and extracted the essence— the lotus endowed with fragrance— O Lord of Gods.
Seeing this auspicious lotus-form, I am struck with wonder and filled with joy;
is it the root of a lotus, or is it something eternal, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns?
Later, when he beheld the Lord in the form of Śiva in the midst of that [vision],
he saw in His hand a wondrous, pure book—
this scripture of the Vīrāgama, for those devotees who perform meritorious deeds.
In this world, there are excellent forms of Śiva-worship; however, due to the lack of a physical support for them,
mental worship is superior, as is the ritual worship of the sacred seat (*pīṭha*),
as well as the worship of a temporary (*kṣipra*) or artificial *liṅga*, and likewise recollection (*smaraṇa*) and meditative visualization (*bhāvana*).
Such are the various types of worship; one must not move the Śivaliṅga. By breaking a consecrated liṅga, one shall go to the Raurava hell.
O Great Goddess, having seen this, I have declared it even to the gods.
The body is one thing, Śiva is another, and the vital breath is yet another; thus she stands established.
Therefore, O gods and asuras, out of compassion I shall tell you:
just as there is fragrance in a flower, so too is there the *liṅga* within the body.
One should not move the consecrated bone during the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) until the ritual is complete;
for one who breaks the *liṅga* incurs a great sin, therefore one must not disturb the worship of the pedestal.
Just as the mantra has been thoroughly practiced within the center of the body,
so too are the *liṅga* and the body [united] as this very *prāṇaliṅga*.
It is like the radiance of the sun or the rays of the moon.

Just as heat is established in fire, coldness in water, strength in wind, the sound of space, sweetness in milk, the tree in its seed, and the sprout in the seed— so too, O virtuous ones, is the auspicious Liṅga of Śiva established within the body.
O Pārvatī, all human beings who desire liberation should perform the worship of the sacred seats (pīṭha);
the fruit of worship performed for ten million kalpas is thereby accomplished.
Thus, out of compassion for them, the *prāṇaliṅga* was revealed;
therefore, it is known in the Śaiva Āgama as well as in the *Trikau*.

Having observed that the scriptures were difficult to comprehend, and especially the *prāṇaliṅga*, the Supreme Person, Hari— Nārāyaṇa, who dwells with Lakṣmī— having heard [this] and abandoned his abode, slept in the Ocean of Milk.
Having reached the peak of Kailāsa, he performed austerities while remaining without a seat.
For what purpose has the Lord of Ramā, becoming tranquil through penance, been performing it for thousands of divine years directed toward me? Tell me this.
"Thus, O Viṣṇu, my installation has been performed; I am manifest before you, O Lord of Umā.
Nārāyaṇa said:
"The worship of Vīraśaiva is meritorious, bestowing the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation."
O Great Lord, please tell me all of that which I desire to know.
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇa, to this most excellent and glorious Vīraśaiva [tradition],
consisting of the six *daṇḍas*, the *maṭha*, the *mudrās*, and the worship of the *āsanas*.
Discipline, tranquility, right conduct, and meditation-yoga whose essence is Śiva;
being a devotee, a worshiper of Maheśvara, one who is gracious, one for whom the *prāṇaliṅga* is his life-breath,
one who has sought refuge, and oneness with the Śivaliṅga— these six petals are dear to me.
Having perceived the mobile linga, as well as the inseparable nature and consciousness, those wise ones and those people are the foremost among devotees;
for the mobile linga is indeed characterized by human conduct and honor.
All those people who abandon the place of enjoyment while wandering about,
and those who are diseased, impure, lame, blind, or afflicted by leprosy and foul deformity—
those people who always perceive with their intellect are known as true devotees.
Having seen one who wears sacred ash, rudrākṣas, a skull-bowl, and the five mudrās,
and having bowed to them, he is called the best of devotees.
Those who avoid what is not offered and what is unfit for consumption, as well as backbiting and anger—
even in their minds— are my devotees and dear to me.
O Maheśvarī, those who are the best among devotees perceive the Guru, the living being (jaṅgama), the Liṅga, and likewise the ancestors with an equal mind.
One should perform the consecration of Śiva, worship, prostration, and circumambulation.
They perform the offering of incense, lamps, and other food offerings as a sign of devotion.
Refined food, a bed, a vehicle, clothing, a fan, and sandals.
Thus, this is the characteristic of a devotee among both stationary and moving beings:
[the possession of] an auspicious vessel, a water-pot, a palm-leaf fan, a deer-skin, a staff, earrings, a patched garment, and so forth, as well as a water-jar and fruits.
Grant this to those who are your devotees; such indeed should be the characteristic of a devotee.
The gift of life, the gift of land, the gift of a daughter, and the gift of gold—
those people who fulfill whatever desire one has are the leaders of devotees.
Blaming Śiva, blaming one's guru, reviling the Āgamas,
and incurring debt by handing over wealth— having done these things, one is not born again as a human being.
Those people who are betrayers of their vows, betrayers of their gurus, and betrayers of Śiva go to the Raurava hell and are further reborn as Caṇḍālas.
If even a devotee of Śiva engages in sexual intercourse with the wife of his guru, the wife of another, or the wife of a Brahmin, he will become deluded by Śiva.
Where is liquor and where is devotion to Śiva? Where is meat and where is the worship of Śiva? For those who are addicted to fish and meat, Śaṅkara remains far away.
A woman in her menses, one who is fierce, one afflicted with leprosy,
a widow, and a maidservant— these are the characteristics of a Caṇḍālī for the sake of sexual pleasure.
One must not eat the leftovers of others, eat together with them, engage in theft, or live by harming living beings; these should not be done by devotees, for if one does so, they become a sinner.
Salutation is one thing and praise is another; apart from Hara, these should not be performed for anyone else by devotees, for if one does so, they become a sinner.
Any person who reviles devotees, reviles the guru, reviles virtuous women, or reviles ascetics will become an enemy of Śiva;
for they likewise revile the lunar days, the weekdays, the asterisms, the yogas, and the karaṇas.
Having meditated upon the entire doctrine of Śiva, one should contemplate the characteristics of a devotee of Śiva.
Poverty and prosperity, death and likewise life—one should constantly contemplate all this as being by the command of Śiva; this is the characteristic mark of devotion.
Pilgrimage to sacred sites, religious observances, the duty of giving, and austerity— all these,
as well as the worship of Śiva, are the supreme characteristics of a devotee.
Nārāyaṇa appeared directly as the lord of the three worlds;
the lord of the three worlds appeared directly as Nārāyaṇa.
The four-faced one is indeed the counter-form of the formless God;
by him alone is this creation produced again and again.
The gods and asuras are called "formless" because their body hairs have arisen from merit.
Through these very three within the triple world, the world arises as the agent;
O great-souled ones, we bow to the formless Lord who is the leader.
O Great Goddess, the Moon and Sun wander as the embodiments of Time;
these are the forms of Maheśa, the formless Lord of the Heart.
The four Vedas, the six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍaṅga), the science of mantras, the Śiva-āgamas,
the science of arts and crafts (śilpaśāstra), astrology, and the sixty-four arts (kalās) follow from this.

O Śiva, by me have not been heard the primary doctrines of the Vāmas, Pāśupatas, Kāpālikas, Bhairavas, Siddhas, Bauddhas, Jains, and the infinite others— the formless teachings of Śaṅkara that pervade the ten directions.
The lords of the assembly of sages attained the formless state through meditation on name and form;
likewise, all the oceans, the five elements, and the mandalas were produced. Through the perfection of the principles (tattva-siddhi), the yogic powers and accomplishments became the domain of Śiva.
In this way, wherever such manifold devotion shines forth,
it is the supreme characteristic of devotion for men who possess the *prāṇaliṅga*:
devotion to Śiva, constant devotion, and devotion to the *jaṅgama* (the living guru).
Devotion to the Guru, devotion to the mantra, and likewise devotion to the sacred ash;
devotion to the limbs [of the deity], devotion to ritual action, and thereafter devotion to worship;
as well as devotion to the grace [bestowed], and likewise devotion toward the one who bestows that grace.
Devotion toward the water for washing the feet, and likewise devotion at the time of the ritual observance.
Devotion to the ancestors, devotion to virtue, and devotion to knowledge, O Maheśvarī.
In this very [state] are faith, devotion, truthfulness, and likewise benevolence.
Devotion to the Eldest and constant devotion to the Accomplished One—these are remembered as the eighteen types of devotion.
Devotion to the one worthy of refuge; devotion to alms, to a maiden, and likewise to a begging bowl; devotion to staffs and earrings; devotion to sacred fords, O Maheśvarī;
devotion to giving, devotion to what is beneficial, and devotion throughout the three worlds.
[Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Plane of Devotion," concerning the relationship with the Prāṇaliṅga, in the Sahasrakoṭi-saṃhitā of the Vīraśaiva Āgama.]
The Plane of Maheśvara.
I shall indeed proclaim this Māheśvara [teaching] for the benefit of all the worlds—
for the gods, asuras, and humans, and for the sages of meritorious deeds.
Especially for my devotees, O Maheśvara, [I shall explain] the sequence of ritual procedures.
The Śiva-mantra, meditation on Śiva, service to a devotee of Śiva,
praise of Śiva, hymns of praise, and the auspicious worship and adoration of Śiva.
The worship of the Śivaliṅga is indeed remembered as the practice of a Māheśvara.
Therefore, O Maheśvara, the qualities of honoring others, authoritative means of knowledge, truthful speech, and service to the guru shall come to be mine.
One who has conquered the senses, who undertakes virtuous actions, and is devoted to the knowledge of Śiva.
O Maheśvarī, I am indeed devoid of both good deeds and evil deeds.
Subsisting on alms, performing pure ablutions and ash-baths born of mantra,
they are dispassionate, stainless, and peaceful, dwelling in the temple of the deity.
They know the Rudrākṣa to be the manifestation of Kanyā and the quality of Maheśvara.
The union with the *liṅga* itself, free from the conduct of the [lower] *kula*,
and a state of tranquility and gentleness of mind— this is remembered as the quality of a devotee of Maheśvara.

The state of Maheśvara becomes one that is unblinking, free from desire, characterized by profound meditation, and pure in essence; it is eternal bliss, self-sufficient, the supreme auspiciousness of perpetual worship, the constant bath, and the supportless nature of His qualities.
Abstaining from the wealth of others, the food of others, and union with the wives of others,
as well as avoiding the speech of others and foolishness— this is the quality of a devotee of Maheśvara.
Matted hair, sacred ash, saffron robes, a loincloth, and the staff—
wherever these five insignia are found, O Maheśvarī, one is truly contented. Likewise, speaking kindly to devotees is considered the true hermitage of devotion.
One should eat the food from the house of a devotee, seek association with devotees,
take delight in the water used for washing the feet of a devotee, be intent upon the remnants of a devotee's offerings,
have a mind engaged in the service of devotees, and contemplate the assemblies of devotees.
Devotees of Maheśvara shall always possess curiosity for the truth;
truth, purity, forgiveness, and wisdom, as well as matted hair and the smearing of ashes.
Subsisting on alms-food is indeed remembered as the quality of a devotee of Maheśvara.
[One should also possess] a maiden, earrings, a vessel, a rudrākṣa, a rosary of beads,
a bamboo staff, a gentle mass of matted hair, a deerskin, and a cow-hair girdle.
The sandals, the turban, and likewise Oḍḍiyāṇa are so described.
The worship and adoration of the Guru, the offering of curd, meditation on Śiva, and the worship of Śiva;
the wearing of a loincloth (or the avoidance of women), pilgrimage, and abstention from meat; being free from both merit and sin—this is the supreme station of the moving (jaṅgama).
Devoid of family customs and stripped of its clan name,
the son is the supreme, peaceful servant of the guru— a moving piece of ground.
Whether in a dwelling or in a forest, one who is free from desire and anger and is constantly devoted to the worship of Śiva is the most excellent living sacred site.
Devotion to Maheśvara has arisen as a pair that brings pleasure to the Liṅga;
there is joy and bliss in the moving [Liṅga], O Śambhu Sadāśiva,
as well as in the Maheśvara hymn and likewise in the Maheśvara mantra.
The worship is indeed Māheśvara, and likewise the meditation is Māheśvara;
even the ritual action is Māheśvara—for they know everything to be Māheśvara.
O Śivā, they declare that he who constantly maintains the state of Maheśa everywhere within his heart is indeed the "Maheśvara-petal."
[Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Glory of the Prāṇaliṅga and of Men Possessing the Prāṇaliṅga," in the Sahasrakoṭi-saṃhitā of the Śrīvīraśaiva Āgama.]
A gift of grace.
Now, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the great [treatise] called Prasāda,
which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men who are devotees and wearers of the prāṇaliṅga.
He always spoke of grace;
he spoke of the grace of the Supreme Lord and the grace of the Supreme Self.
O Goddess of the gods, [I offer] the grace of the Guru, especially that of the *jaṅgama* (living embodiments),
the grace of the *prāṇaliṅga*, and the grace of the devotees of Śiva.
He correctly described the remnants of what had been eaten by the Guru, the Para-guru, the Parāpara-guru, and furthermore, the Parameṣṭhi-guru.
At that very time today, he bestows the grace known as Prasāda, which destroys all evil;
being impartial, he grants that Prasāda continuously.
O Maheśvarī, the grace of Śiva destroys the sins of all;
the grace of the Guru is supreme, destroying even the slayer of a Brahmin and bringing peace to all defects.
It eternally bestows enjoyment and liberation, destroys all adversities,
pacifies all diseases, and is the supreme bringer of all peace. It grants all perfections, is pure, and destroys the sins of all births.
It is eternally composed of all bliss, the destroyer of all heart-diseases,
the cause of the eight supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā* for those seeking victory,
the bestower of sons and grandsons upon men, and the dispeller of the fear of famine.
It is the cause for the destruction of fear from the nine planets and the piśācas.
It bestows upon men mastery over kings, mastery over subjects, mastery over women, and mastery over spirits;
it grants immortality, perfection of speech, and perfection of the body.
It bestows the power of moving through the underworld, as well as traveling through the sky;
it provides auspicious alchemy (*rasāyana*) and the attainment of the perfected sword (*khaḍgasiddhi*).
It likewise grants the vision of Vetālas and Bhairavas, as well as Kāpālikas,
and provides the sight of Siddhas such as Vīrabhadra and others.
O Maheśvarī, for those men who possess the *prāṇaliṅga*,
the grace of the *jaṅgama* (the living liṅga) redeems ten million members of their lineage.
[The merit of] bathing at sacred fords, recitation, meditation, sacrifice, the gift of a cow, and the gift of a bull— [all these are attained through the grace of the *jaṅgama*].
He also performed the consecration of ten million lingas and constructed ten millions of tanks.
The installation of ten million Brahmins, the granting of ten million maidens,
the worship of ten million Lingas, and austerity practiced for ten million years are all equal in merit.
All that is accomplished with ease by those of meritorious deeds.
Those who joyfully consume the water from his feet and the food given through his grace— the Lord of Nāśana fully obtains all of that through his favor.
Therefore, O beloved, it is said that for wandering ascetics,
"prasāda" refers solely to the food remaining after they have eaten.
With the meritorious water from the feet of Śiva, and through His grace,
the bathing of one’s own Prāṇaliṅga must be performed with the food offering (naivedya);
there is no fault in this, as I have sworn this three times.
If he commits a sin, even that sinner goes to hell;
yet, if he acts with devotion toward his own *liṅga*, he incurs no fault whatsoever.
In other cases, wherever he commits an offense, he shall indeed be subject to punishment.
He is to be slain by the king, by the servants of Yama, by me, by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, by the world-protectors, and by the spirits; indeed, he must be punished.
The Guru and the living being (jaṅgama) are indeed the worship of the Śivaliṅga;
likewise, one should partake of the water from their feet and the food remaining after they have eaten.
One should consume the *prasāda* of the devotees of Śiva for the purification of one's birth;
[one should also consume] the remnants of the Guru, the remnants of Śiva, and the speech of the *jaṅgama*.
For whomsoever there is a defect of speech regarding all these, their state as a bound soul (*paśutva*) becomes certain.
Proper devotion to the Guru, to all living beings at all times, and constant devotion to Śiva— this is called the state of prasāda (divine grace) as food.
One should not abandon food that has been offered, nor likewise the living beings belonging to one's guru.
O Great Goddess, by uttering "Siddhe Siddhe," one obtains the fruit of worshipping ten million *liṅgas*.
One should offer the *prasāda* and the food offering (*naivedya*) of the *jaṅgama*;
indeed, the soul is purified by the *prasāda* of the *prāṇaliṅga*, and not otherwise.
The water for the foot-washing, the supreme food remaining from the meal,
the consecrated water, the food offering, and the grace— these belong to the Prāṇaliṅginī.
O Dear One, by the grace of this water, it removes epilepsy, mental anguish, all diseases, poisons, and planetary afflictions for those devoted to Śiva.
It removes poison, diseases, and piśācas, as well as fevers and other ailments.

One should eat food offered through divine grace; truth leads to all-encompassing peace. Even the sinner, the inhabitant of hell, and likewise the killer of a Brahmin—through the grace of Maheśvara’s food, one truly becomes pure and composed of bliss.
He who eats beef, drinks liquor, and consumes human flesh immediately becomes a spirit-souled being and is glorified in the world of Śiva.
The theft of Brahman’s property becomes the theft of the gods; one who steals the gifts offered to others incurs the same sin. By consuming the *prasāda* of devotees, one becomes pure.
Yet, by disparaging the *prasāda*, one remains impure even for hundreds of millions of kalpas.
That evil person goes to hell; no one in his lineage shall be a savior.
The water from washing the feet is sacred, as is the food remaining after a meal;
for all such faults, there shall be expiation.
O Maheśvarī, the water from washing the feet is sacred, as is the food remaining after a meal.
He who accepts food out of faith is liberated from great sin;
O Śivā, bathing at all sacred fords such as the Gaṅgā is equaled by bathing in the water used for washing [the deity’s] feet.
By eating the remnants of the food already consumed, you shall attain union with Śiva.
The water from the feet of those who are mobile destroys sin;
this grace is for the sake of attaining liberation—this is the truth spoken by the Lord.

He performs with compassion the salutation of the moving beings, prepares a seat, washes their feet, offers clothing, incense, flowers, and other items, as well as food, incense smoke, lamps, and hymns of praise.
That man, freed from all defects, attains heaven.
O Śaṅkarī, having abandoned worldly conduct and family customs, as well as all hesitation,
that devotee attains the status of being the creator of all the gods.
O Ambikā, whatever worship of Śiva one performs through mind, action, or speech,
as well as devotion toward the mobile [deities], all that must be performed.
Whether he be a Caṇḍāla, a twice-born, or others from any other lineage,
upon seeing the Śiva-mudrā, one who is devoted to Śiva should circumambulate it for a long distance and purify his food, clothing, and so forth.
O Supreme Goddess, that devotee is liberated from all sins.
Having learned the greatness of prasāda from the mouth of a guru,
or having heard it through the scriptures of the Śiva-āgamas or through the teachings of the Śivadharma;
O fair-faced one, grace is always secret; it is the truth, the absolute truth. Through grace, having been freed from all sins, one shall attain Śiva.
[Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The State of Grace regarding the Connections with the Prāṇaliṅga," in the *Sahasrakoṭisaṃhitā* of the *Śrīvīraśaivāgama*.]
The Seal of the Life-force (Prāṇaliṅga)
Now, O Great Goddess, my beloved, I shall speak of the *prāṇaliṅga*.
For all men at all times, for the gods, the enemies of the gods,
for the sages, the yakṣas, the nāgas, the siddhas, and the brahmins;
O beloved, for the sake of enjoyment and liberation, there are indeed various types of *liṅgas*:
the *jyotirliṅga* belongs to the gods, the *ātmaliṅga* to the yogins,
the *svayaṃbhuliṅga* to the *nāgas*, and the *ūrdhvaliṅga* to the great-souled ones.
Of the Vasus, who possess the mark of immortality, he is the one among the sages who bears the mark of Brahman.
The Bāṇaliṅga is for men, and the Mukhaliṅga is for Vaiśyas.
The linga of the Śūdras is made of clay; that of the Rākṣasas is a yoga-linga;
the linga of Surendra is of gold; and that of Havirbhuj (Agni) is of topaz.
The *trapuṣa* is the *liṅga* of Yama; that which is made of *putra* is for Nirṛti; the one called *pravā* belongs to Varuṇa; and the *gomedaka-liṅga* belongs to Vāyu.
The linga of Kubera is made of the jewel of the earth and is endowed with all splendors;
the linga of Rudra is silver, and that of Brahmā is a linga of light.
There is the blue linga of Indra and that of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
O Goddess of the gods, the Liṅga of Rudra known as Iṣṭakāmeśvara is endowed with nine gems;
however, the Mantra-liṅga of Īśvara is even greater.
The great preeminent Tāra-liṅga of Śiva, the Supreme Self,
is the most excellent among the eighty-four million liṅgas; indeed,
it is the pearl-liṅga of the Moon and the lotus-liṅga of the Sun, which is auspicious.
The followers of Śiva know the Brahma-liṅga to be the supreme among the Īśānas.
And for the hermitages of the Pāśupatas, there is the fivefold-temple Liṅga;
for all those who observe the Great Vow (Mahāvratin), there is the Lord Bhuvaneśvara.
The *cit-liṅga* belongs to those who have attained the state of *kāma-mukha*; the *śakti-liṅga* belongs to the *vāmas*;
and the *prāṇa-liṅga* especially belongs to all castes (*varṇas*).
O friend, these are the names of the fourfold types of *liṅgas*.
Of the four perfected ones (siddhas) residing on Śrīśaila on earth at the four monasteries (maṭhas)—
of the true guru named Revaṇa, of his disciple Marueśa, and of that great-souled Siddha— [there is] the Śāntamalleśvara Liṅga.
The *liṅga* named Kapila Siddheśvara is proclaimed to belong to him;
it is declared to be the *bhoga-liṅga* of the perfected one (siddha) Rāmadeva.
And the auspicious Cennamalleśvara belongs to the meritorious Paṇḍitārādhya.
This fourfold division has been shown according to the path of the Vedas:
the four Siddhas, the four Vedas, and Girīśvara as the lord of the four gates;
[the deity] endowed with the six supports (bharaṇas) and the six lords who sustain the six locations.

The armpit (*kakṣa*) and the palm of the hand (*karasthala*), as well as the visible part of the head (*mūrdhamāṅgāvalokyaka*); the measure of the arm (*bāhu*) is the extent from the shoulder to the elbow (*vuranarjamiti*), which serves as the indicator for wearing the *liṅga*; and the palm of the hand (*karasthala*) is the region of the ear (*turavaṇamaru*) and the visible part.
The deity Rāma is Maheśvara, who bears the *liṅga* upon his spoken limb.
O Ambikā, one should always wear the illustrious Paṇḍitārādhyaka at the base of the arms; one should constantly maintain the presence of the Liṅga in the palate;
and one should perpetually establish the presence of the Jaṅgamas between the eyebrows.
O beautiful lady, the essence of literature is indeed like a mantra at the tip of the nose;
O lady, let there be no separation from the literature born of the *liṅga* and the *jaṅgama*.
O my beloved, I shall now describe the general rule for this very matter.
O Pārvatī, one should worship the Jyotirliṅga, the Manoliṅga, the Prāṇaliṅga,
and the renowned Guruliṅga— indeed, all liṅgas.
Among all these signs, the *prāṇaliṅga* is preeminent.
Just as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) pervades the body, so too the *prāṇaliṅga* is not a mere external union.
It is like oil in sesame seeds, ghee in milk, or the meaning within a word, and the stability of the mind.
While all the senses remain centered in the mind,
those devoted to the Prāṇaliṅga continue their investigation for that very duration.
First is the Guru, then Śiva, followed by devotion and the vision of the rule (samaya);
O Goddess, each one of these is individually a life-force-liṅga (prāṇaliṅga).
The worship of the sacred seats (pīṭha), the immobile, the mental,
the quick-liṅga, the momentary-liṅga, the divine-liṅga, and likewise the fiery-liṅga.
The wind has the liṅga of wood, water has the liṅga of earth,
and the self-born has the liṅga of the self; O Śāmbhavī, there is also the golden liṅga,
as well as those made of gomedaka, crystal, pearl, lapis lazuli, and emerald.
To whom does a linga made of sapphire belong, and those made of copper,
lead, tin, iron, wood, deodar, or sandalwood?
O Śivā, the fruit, the earthen linga, the flour-made one, the leaf-made one,
the one fashioned from kāntālaka, the turmeric-colored one, and that made from the moon (silver)—
these and many other types of lingas are fashioned by the perfected yogins.
The word of the Guru, the Linga, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings,
and all the deities beginning with Brahmā, exist as that which is fashioned for the sake of desire.
O beloved, such signs as these exist in abundance for men who possess the *prāṇaliṅga*; their *liṅga* is indeed the *liṅga* of Śrīśaila.
Alternatively, they know these two—the Bāṇaliṅga and the Mukhya—to be the primary ones;
all other liṅgas are indeed fashioned from natural materials.
O beautiful one, worship performed with this multitude of liṅgas is eternally auspicious.
The fruit of worship indeed belongs to that Śrīśaila Liṅga;
through seeing it, touching it, remembering it, and furthermore hearing of it,
one obtains the fruit of worship from the Śrīśaila Liṅga.
Therefore, this linga originating from Śrīśaila belongs indeed to those who possess the linga of their vital breath (prāṇa).
I shall proclaim the fruit of worship; listen to it in its true nature, O Pārvatī. Worship is correctly said to be threefold: *sāva*, *śāntava*, and *samya*.
That which is accompanied by a lamp is *sāva*, and sacrificial food (*haviṣyānna*) is *śāntava*.
It is said that [the rite] ends with the *samyagbali*, and worship is declared to be threefold.

The worship of the *pīṭha* yields a hundred thousand-fold fruit; that of a stationary (*sthāvara*) [liṅga] yields a hundred thousand times ten million; that of a mental (*mānasa*) [liṅga] yields a hundred times ten million; that of a *kṣipra-liṅga* yields a thousandfold;
and that of the *ātma-liṅga* or the *padma-liṅga* is incalculable when performed.
The Liṅga in the sky beyond the millions, endowed with stars and the like, is beyond the range of perception.
All various forms of worship are for the sake of worldly enjoyment;
however, the instruction regarding the *prāṇaliṅga* is obtained through the merit of thousands of births.
Indeed, the path of the *prāṇaliṅga*, which was previously concealed, is now revealed.
In the meantime, during the period of the great dissolution,
in that most terrible destruction at the end of the aeon, when all things had merged into the auspicious Śiva,
the Lord of Ramā was subsequently instructed on the peak of Kailāsa.
The greatness of the *prāṇaliṅga* has been correctly declared by me:
in the beginning, during the Kṛta Yuga, it was Śambhu; in the Tretā Yuga, the Four-faced One (Brahmā);
in the Dvāpara Yuga, Vāsudeva; and in the Kali Yuga, all the great sages.
O Maheśānī, from the sages [came] the guardians of the directions, all the deities, the yakṣas, gandharvas, siddhas, those of the Garuḍa lineage, and the kinnaras;
and in their midst were Sukheśī and Viśvakeśī, along with Nandin.
Tripurā, the presiding deity over the three cities, having known her as one extracted from all virtues,
understood the path of deceit and the characteristics of the *prāṇaliṅga*.
O Goddess of gods, by that very [knowledge] she was conquered in mind through his grace.

Tripurā, the sovereign of Tripura, was filled with pride due to her devotion to Śiva. Because she was the cause of his destruction, you became the sound in the form of a wise man (Budha). By Hari in the form of Budha, those Rākṣasas were deluded.
Therefore, O Great Goddess, by casting off devotion in this way, the three cities (Tripura) shall be destroyed by the power of the Rākṣasa who has assumed the form of a bee;
there is nothing on earth equal to the worship of the Prāṇaliṅga.
The glorious wearer of the *prāṇaliṅga* is the Great Lord Maheśvara himself;
he is Brahmā, he is Śiva, Viṣṇu, Śūdra, and all the deities.
This *prāṇaliṅga* is the manifest God, the husband of Śivā.
O Śivā, even a Brāhmaṇa of noble lineage, if devoid of the worship of the Liṅga, is equal to anyone of another caste; this which has been spoken by the Lord is the truth.
One born of another caste may be a devotee; even he may become equal to a Brahmin.
Such a person, though fallen from the status of a woman or Rudra, should wear the *prāṇaliṅga*.
O Brahmins, those of noble birth and sons who perform meritorious deeds have achieved their purpose through such virtuous action.
Just as a body bitten by a snake becomes possessed by the serpent,
so too does a body marked by the *liṅga* become possessed by the *liṅga*.
And the *liṅga* bestowed by the Guru, once placed in the hand, remains outside the hand.
Therefore, the piercing of the *liṅga*—the *prāṇaliṅga*—must indeed be maintained;
thus do all the scriptures, spoken by Śiva, declare. O Dear One, even ten million Śiva temples, when purified by this, become sanctified.
The subtle body (liṅgadeha) does not undergo consecration; likewise, it is said that [the body] is real and consists of six elements.
However, without the subtle body, digging [the ground] and performing worship for it is fruitless.
This applies to the Śiva-āgama, Tantra, Yāmala, Yoga, and Vaiṣṇava traditions regarding the altar (vedi).

"The scripture proceeds with the statement, 'Even though it is ancient, there is a prohibition. Thereafter, having properly constructed a cave-mouth, a pavilion, or a temple of Śiva according to one's means alone, perform the rite of the lamp."
And likewise, he should cause the mobile devotees to receive permission.
Revaṇa, Marusiddha, Rāmadeva,
and Paṇḍitārādhya— these are the lords of sages of the four monasteries (maṭhas).
Through the very sequence of traditional succession, these devotees of Śiva [established] the Jaṅgamas.
Having worshipped according to the rule, one should perform the rite of the *vibhūti-viṭikā*.
Having performed the subsequent rite, one should provide food on each respective occasion—
whether after one day, three days, five days,
nine days, ten days, a fortnight, a month, or even a year.

The *rudra-śrāddha* is for the twice-born (*dvijāti*), the *śiva-śrāddha* for kings, the *jīva-śrāddha* for Vaiśyas, and it likewise exists for others. One should feed Brahmins who are devoted to that particular caste, as well as devotees of Śiva.
And it is possible for a Brāhmaṇa who has eaten elsewhere to give even a mere portion of food to devotees of other castes;
at the end of the meal, he should offer betel, perfumes, flowers, and incense.
May he grant to the devotees of Śiva food according to their desire,
and especially to those Brāhmaṇas who possess devotion to Śiva,
clothing, gold, rings, umbrellas, ornaments, and sandals.
Having given [the gifts], performed circumambulation, and prostrated, he received a blessing. Then, having filled vessels made of rice flour with ghee and fashioned wicks from cotton threads,
he offered various kinds of lamps to his preceptor.
The monkey approached the devotee of Śiva together with the villagers and the brāhmaṇas;
having made a great offering to Śiva, the Supreme Soul,
he placed a lamp-vessel upon his head and performed three circumambulations.
Furthermore, everyone should begin the recitation of benedictions at the temple of Śiva.
One shall go to the world of Śiva, the foremost among all knowers of the Vedas;
thereafter, one should properly circumambulate the abode of Śiva,
and again, having caused the gift of betel-leaf to be given according to one's pleasure.
[Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Section on the Prāṇaliṅga," in the Sahasrakoṭi-saṃhitā of the Śrī Vīraśaiva Āgama.]
The gift of refuge.
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the great [treatise] named Śaraṇa,
which is a refuge for all the gods, a forest of death for the enemies of the gods,
a means for the devotees of Śiva, and a crossing over the ocean of worldly existence.
Proclaiming "Śaraṇa" removes the accumulation of sins;
performing the worship of Śiva brings the beautiful bride of liberation;
and the worship of the Liṅga, renowned for its five mudrās, is likewise [efficacious].
By the mere sight of you, O refuge for those seeking refuge,
even one of evil conduct becomes a wise man who follows the path of right conduct.
Upon seeing a mobile *liṅga*, which is a refuge for those seeking refuge,
one should not make distinctions based on caste— whether one is a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, Śūdra, or even a Caṇḍāla; if one does so, one shall become a denizen of hell.
Whether one wears the Śiva-linga or is devoid of merit, provided one is initiated;
For the sake of initiation, that pure *liṅga* and the pure mantra were [bestowed] by the Great-Souled One. All those excellent Brāhmaṇas declare the Nigamas and Āgamas:
"By austerity (*tapas*), sin is destroyed; by [austerity], the lineage of the lowly is purified."
In the midst of the flow of the Gaṅgā,
one who possesses a subtle body (liṅgadehī) and is a purified soul shall be born into the lineage of Śiva; in such a case,
neither birth, family, learning, or virtuous conduct is taken into account.
The matted locks, the sectarian mark (vibhūti), the liṅga, and the sight of the rudrākṣa— by the mere sight of these, one should perform a prostration with joy, which is dear to the Guru.
[One should also worship] the aśvattha, śamī, and bilva trees, as well as the solar disc.
Śiva is eternally present in the preceptor, in the Śivaliṅga, in the hearts of devotees,
and in the sacrificial enclosure of the Agnihotra;
therefore, [He is likewise present] in the moving forms [of His devotees].
The *liṅga* measured by the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the characteristic of oneness with the *Śivaliṅga*;
the *liṅga* that fills the space of the three worlds is perfectly filled within the body.
That very thing is the characteristic of the oneness of the Great Goddess with the Śiva-liṅga;
likewise, for the moving [deities], it is the foot, as well as the characteristic of the conduct of the covenant (samaya).
For the mantra, it is the syllable, the foot, devotion, and the collection of mantras.
The refuge of monasteries is indeed the feet; the refuge of alms-food is the Lord;
the refuge of right conduct is likewise [the Lord]; and the supreme refuge is bliss.
The refuge known as devotion and knowledge, likewise that called detachment;
the refuge of the Vedas and the wonderful refuge of initiation;
the refuge known as purity of devotion, and the refuge of the supreme goal.
And indeed, the refuge of Maheśvara is the eternal refuge of grace.
The refuge known as Prāṇaliṅga, the refuge known as Śaraṇa,
the refuge of oneness with Śiva, and the supreme refuge of oneness with the Liṅga.
The unity of the vital breath and the *liṅga* is the refuge; it is designated as the refuge for those who have become mendicants.
The refuge known as Nātha, the supreme refuge known as Haṃsa,
the refuge of Oṃkāra, and the refuge designated as Tattva.
Taking refuge in the Siddhānta and taking refuge in Vīraśaivism—
thus is refuge declared in that which is known as the Rahasyāgama.
All this has been declared by me out of affection for you, O fair-faced one;
having thus learned from the mouth of the Guru the worship of the Prāṇaliṅga, the Guru [should perform it].
[Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Refuge," in the Śrī Vīrāgama, the compendium of ten million verses.]
The Section on the Unity with the Śiva-liṅga.
Initiation (dīkṣā) is declared to be the gift to the devotee, and thereafter the gift to the devotee of Maheśvara.
The *māheśvara* mantra is the mixed word of the two minds;
it is called the "petal of grace" (*prasādadala*), the sprout of the mantra of grace.
The auspicious *prāṇaliṅga* is the very life of Śiva;
they say that the great practice known as *caraṇa* consists of a hundred forms of right conduct.
O lady of excellent complexion, the supreme mantra is the oneness of devotion, and the oneness of the mantra is the oneness of [the self].
Through grace, the oneness of the vital breath and the *liṅga* is certainly established for one who has taken refuge.
The unity of refuge, the superiority of Śiva, the unity, the sixfold support, devotion, and likewise the support itself— this, O Maheśvarī, is the foundation of Your own abode.

The wise know Prasāda, Maṇipūra, Prāṇaliṅga, Anāhata, Śaraṇa, Viśuddhi-kamala, and Ājñā as the bestower of oneness; Liṅga is declared to be the bestower of devotion, and Mantramāheśvara is the bestower of restraint.
In the supreme Self, during the meditation on grace, the *prāṇaliṅga* [is established].

In the case of the two, Śiva and Śivā, the refuge is the phallic emblem (liṅga) and the garland; the oneness of the two is the phallic emblem. Fire conjoined with water, as well as the flower and the fragrance in the object, and the fragrance of sandalwood—this is the characteristic of the oneness of the Śiva-liṅga.
The *liṅga* is commensurate with the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the vital breath is commensurate with the *liṇga*;
because of their inseparable relationship, the characteristic of Śiva and the *liṅga* is oneness.
Whether it be stationary or moving upon the earth, let one fashion it as the Śiva-liṅga.
The linga is commensurate with the vital breath (prāṇa), characterized by its identity with the Śiva-linga.
The three worlds fill the sky, and the body is completely filled within the *liṅga*;
O Great Goddess, that indeed is the characteristic of the unity of the universal *liṅga*.
The light of vision is in the ear, and likewise the sense of smell is in the nostrils;
sweetness is in the tongue—this is the characteristic of the unity of Śiva and the individual soul (iṅga).
The stationary and the moving, filled with the nature of space—
thus all is pervaded by Śiva, characterized by its identity with the Śivaliṅga.
One should meditate with a state free from conceptual construction upon the mobile linga;
for the gods who are devotees of Śiva, the defining characteristic is their oneness with the Śivalinga.
Through the actions of mind, speech, and body, one should not contemplate any deity other than Him.
One should not conceive of any difference between the Guru and the *jaṅgama* (the living devotee), nor between the *liṅga* and the *jaṅgama*.
Just as one’s own happiness is dear to oneself, so too should one regard the *liṅga* and the *jaṅgama*. Having unified them through the mind and heart, one should not think of anything else at all.
In captivity, in the forest, in a difficult pass, amidst terrible enemies, or in poison—
one should meditate upon Śiva as the Guru-liṅga and utterly destroy all evils.
The *liṅga* is filled with the Self of all; Śiva is filled with the Self of all.
Whether one’s conduct is good or bad, whether one is deficient or a transgressor of the sacred rules (*sūtra*), one should contemplate that by the mere wearing of the *liṅga*, one is indeed Śiva.
Whether it be happiness or suffering, and whether it be a good person or an evil person—so it is.
The supreme moving shrine (jaṅgama-sthala) is to be viewed with equanimity;
subsisting on alms, devotion to Śiva, and service to the moving shrines [are the means].
One should practice detachment and undertake pilgrimages,
whether on foot or by vehicle, combined with worship performed at the three times of day and accompanied by bathing with sacred ash (vibhūti).
Among those who wear matted hair and rudrākṣa beads, the best are those established in the "moving" [state] (jaṅgamastha),
who are free from verbal harshness, mental suffering, anger, and calamity;
they avoid the food of others and the wives of others— such are those established in the "moving" state.

The recitation of the five-syllabled mantra, worship, meditation, and the smearing with sacred ash; the maiden, the water-pot, and the bearer of the supreme mobile and immobile [liṅgas]; free from desire, immovable, peaceful, ageless, and a perpetual worshiper.
O fair-complexioned lady, that gentle one who always subsists on alms is liberated;
he perceives the Linga-pitha as the Great Night, which is Shiva consisting of the five principles.
The *liṅga* purified by the lotus of reality (*tattva*) is declared to be the *prāṇaliṅga*;
the *manoliṅga* is [purified] by the self, and the *adhidaivata-liṅga* by the mantra alone.
In that very way, O Goddess of gods, the characteristic of oneness with the Śivaliṅga arises through devotion to the Guru; thereafter, it is further realized through initiation.

The Māheśvara division is further [divided] by the distinction of mantras; it is called the Śāmbhava Prasāda division, for the attainment of mantra-perfection is the state of grace (prasādatā). According to the rule of association with the *liṅga*, it is remembered as the *prāṇaliṅga*.

O Śāṅkarī, according to the sequence of Śiva’s conduct, one should practice with a sense of oneness: oneness of mantra, oneness of the Śiva-liṅga, oneness with the *jaṅgama* (the living master), and oneness of the vital breath— all within the state of refuge in You as the single supreme Liṅga.
Thus, through merit, there arises the singular oneness with the Śiva-liṅga;
the preeminent mantra is the word of the Guru; the preeminent worship is the station of the Guru;
the preeminent meditation is the form of the Guru; and the preeminent liberation is the grace of the Guru.

[Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Oneness of Śiva and the Liṅga," together with the characteristics of the six petals, in the *Sahasrakoṭisaṃhitā* of the *Śrīvīraśaivāgama*.]
Salutation to the venerable Guru, the embodiment of the phallic symbol (liṅga).
The characteristics of the six-petaled [lotus] are the six petals...
First, the *bhakti* petal was composed together with the Siddhas, Suras, and Asuras; after that, the petal called *māheśvara* was fashioned by Brahmā and the Lord of the Devas (Indra);
and furthermore, the divine *prasāda* petal was composed by Viṣṇu through the worship of Śiva.
Afterwards, O Rudra, the petal of the liṅga of consciousness and vital breath was fashioned by thousands.
The petal of unity with Paraśiva was fashioned as that place of refuge, eternally pure through the worship of the manifest Lord (Sākṣādīśvara) and by means of the Śakti-mantras and others.
Thus, in the Vīra-Śivāgamas, the Siddhānta-mantra-pada has been described.
The six-petalled lotus, which is to be honored by others, has a nature of worship and a mind purified [of defilements].
The worship of the Hero (vīrārcana), performed by bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas, was established for that purpose;
the worship of the Liṅga in the heart-center (hṛccakraliṅgārcana) was fashioned specifically for the easy attainment of goals by the sick;
and the worship of the Liṅga with devotion in the solar orb (ravimaṇḍala) was ordained for those of low status.
O King, this worship of the *prāṇaliṅga* was practiced by the Brahmins, Siddhas, Buddhas, and Munis.
The worship of the Jyotirliṅga is for Śiva; the Liṅga made of lotus-paste is for Paśupati; the Liṅga made of sapphire alone is for the Lord Hari;
and the incomparable pearl Liṅga is indeed for the Moon-bearer, Kuvaira.
And they say, O Lord, that there is another form of Mukunda made of gold, known as Pracetas.
O Sage, the lotus-seated [Brahmā] has fashioned a liṅga of vaidūrya; Viṣṇu worships a liṅga of ruby; Īśvara [Śiva] has one made of emerald; and the Sun’s is made of diamond.
Furthermore, the Daityas and the enemies of the gods have liṅgas of tin, while that of the Yakṣas is of lead.
This linga, made of that same metal, was worshipped by wicked piśācas.
O Śivā, in this way the stone-born liṅga is always worshipped by mortals, while that prāṇaliṅga is worshipped within the lotus-petal of the heart by the lords of yogis.
By these very means, gods, asuras, and humans constantly attain the supreme state;
therefore, one should directly perceive that which is called Maheśa through the insights declared in the Vedas and the Śiva Āgamas.
The Determination of the Partless Liṅga of Vital Breath (Niṣkala-prāṇaliṅga-nirṇaya):

Formerly, the Siddhas, the lords of gods and asuras, and the sages remained bound by the noose of saṃsāra; they were intent on the twilight prayers, the recitation of the Vedas, and the performance of sacrifices with the three sacred fires.
Having taken refuge at the lotus feet of the illustrious Guru-nātha, those who have attained it go to the supreme state—
the station of the lord of the mountain of the land, which is a wave of the ocean of the nectar of Śaiva knowledge.

Having conquered the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (turya) through the reckoning of reality by means of true knowledge, she remains established in the sovereignty of meditation upon the feet of the Moon-crested Lord alone.

Having transcended the six groups of sense-objects through stainless knowledge, and having fashioned a golden bracelet from the nectar-ocean wave of Śiva-knowledge— which is full of immortality, risen from the honey, and consists of solid consciousness— and having bound it upon the circle of the earth in the palm of his hand;
Having conquered the latent impressions of the transformations of sound and the qualities (*guṇas*), having destroyed the sense of particularity,
and having attained the pure state of Śambhu; remaining within the lotus of differentiation and becoming Śiva,
I abandon this entire body bound by fetters and go to the state of Śiva.
The maiden is distinguished, clad in deerskin and white; she is the ground for the supreme rite, stainless,
and the ornament that bestows the goals of human existence.
The adornment of rudrākṣa beads for those who move upon this earth.

He who was fashioned from gold, silver, and other metals [is now seen] as a begging bowl among alms-vessels; he who was radiant splendor [is now] ashes; and he who was clothed in garments [is now] naked as the directions.
Among the seventy million mantras, the auspicious five-syllabled mantra is supreme;
among the special forms of Śiva-worship, the adoration of the *prāṇaliṅga* is the highest.
In all sacred observances, the supreme Vīramāheśvara is the highest;
and in all ritual forms, the Śivaliṅga is the most exalted.

Having remembered the Lord Manantaram, having made Gaṇapati [one's witness], having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana), having abandoned all openings of the vital breaths (maru) and the three bonds (pāśatraya),
and having severed all mental fluctuations and realized the state of Śambhu—
O living soul, having realized the eternal distinction between yourself and the body, I go to the state of Śiva.

[Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Determination of the Niṣkala Prāṇaliṅga Together with the Characteristics of the Origin of the Six Petals," in the Sahasrakoṭi-saṃhitā of the Śrī Vīraśaiva Āgama.]
The Secret of Vīramaṭha
The Śrī Devī said:
O Supreme Lord, I desire to hear all that secret of the Vīrāgama which bestows the fruit of Vīraśaivism; please tell it to me.

Īśvara said: O beloved, listen to the truth in its entirety regarding the monastery, the lineage, right conduct, the vital breath, the *prāṇaliṅga*, worldly enjoyment, liberation, and spiritual perfection.
O Goddess, O beloved, I shall now describe the four monasteries, the four liṅgas, the excellent grove, the worship of Śiva, the proper conduct, and the ritual sequence.
O Pārvatī, I shall now declare the Siddhas of the Yogapīṭha, Mahāpīṭha, Jñānapīṭha, and Saumyapīṭha, which is established in right conduct.
The pedestal (pīṭha) is declared to be the seat of the liṅga (liṅgāsana), consisting of the petals and the six supports (ādhāra-ṣaṭka).
The monastery (maṭha) is designated by the names of the Siddhas; thus the names of the liṅga are otherwise.
First was the teacher Revana, after him Marala,
then the illustrious sage Ramadeva, and finally the preceptor Panditaradhya.
The names of the Siddhas have also been declared by the Great-Souled One;
O Pārvatī, listen to their characteristics and names, O Paśu.
The great-souled Revaṇa [established] the peaceful Malleśvara Liṅga.
The Liṅga known as Kapila Siddha, Malleśa, is accompanied by hosts of Siddhas.
O Goddess, this has been declared by those who know the scriptures regarding the accomplishment of Marula.
It is declared that the *bhogaliṅga* of Rāmadeva, the lord of sages,
is the Malleśvara Liṅga, which was to be worshipped by that great-souled one.
Likewise, one should state the names of the monasteries (maṭhas) in their proper sequence;
O daughter of the Mountain, I shall now tell you the names of the six [deities].
Devotion to Maheśvara, the grace of the *prāṇaliṅga*,
the feet [of the Guru], and oneness with the Śivaliṅga— these six are dear to me.
O Goddess, the practice of initiation proceeds through the sequence of ever-increasing success.
Through austerity, worship, and devotion, the state of being sixfold has been entered.
O Goddess, [the soul becomes] one who possesses devotion by virtue of initiation (*dīkṣā*), one who awakens to the mantra of Maheśa,
and one who possesses grace (*prasāda*) through the vision of the company of the Liṅga.
O Goddess, the *prāṇaliṅga* belongs to both the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and Śiva;
those who understand the distinction between these two know it as the *prāṇaliṅga*.
Because the manifestation of the self is seen together with its subtle body (liṅga), the leaf is called "shelter" (śaraṇa); therefore it is declared to be the refuge.
O God, the measure of the leaf is the oneness of the subtle body, which distinguishes the individual soul from others.
One should gradually apply everything with the respective substrates and mantras.
One should understand that this is the unity of the *liṅgas* of the six petals in their proper sequence;
having performed the contemplation of the universal self through compassion and with the mind.
For one who perceives [the Self] in the form of pure consciousness, such is the characteristic of devotion:
whether one be an outcaste or even a twice-born, if they possess devotion to Śiva, they are a true ascetic.
Holding that [state] equally with the mind, free from deficiency or excess,
they call that alone, O Goddess, the great state of Māheśvara.
One should always worship those who bear the marks of Śiva, even if they are low-born, with a mind free from thoughts of deficiency or excess.
The place of grace has been declared for them through the gathering of that grace,
having understood the union of the supreme Self and the individual self either from the mouth of a guru or by oneself.
O Supreme Goddess, they know that very [state] as the petal of the *prāṇaliṅga*;
it is the mobility and the movement of both the *liṅga* and the Self. That pair, by virtue of its wandering nature, is declared to be the place of refuge.
The wise one brings about the unity of the six supports, the six chakras, the six-petaled lotus, and the six syllables, making them mutually devoid of differentiation.
The wise call that very oneness with the Śiva-liṅga "Da";
the sequence of the Daḍdalas has been declared—now hear the sequence of the Prāṇaliṅgas.
The Goddess said:
"Externally, the *liṅga* is seen; the vital breath (*prāṇa*) resides within the body.
O Supreme Lord, tell me of the connection between the *prāṇa* and the *liṅga*."
Īśvara said: Water situated within a jar is heated from the outside by a blazing fire;
through the application of the fire’s blaze, the watery element becomes hot.
O Goddess, one should maintain this Root Wheel (mūlacakra) above the navel,
situated in the center of the aperture of space and revealed as the Prāṇaliṅga.
O Goddess, this Wheel of Brahmā (brahmacakra), however, is again below the location of the navel.
Within, the Prāṇaliṅga, which is the essence of the mind, is revealed;
O Goddess, this is the Viṣṇucakra, and this is certainly Maṇipūra.
By means of piercing the path of the Suṣumṇā, the Prāṇaliṅga is revealed.
O Goddess, this is the wheel of Rudra, because it obstructs the path of the wind;
it is revealed as the *prāṇaliṅga* within the unstruck (*anāhata*) state.
O Goddess, this Śiva-cakra is within the lotus of purification;
O Goddess, it is the bond of pure consciousness, the Prāṇa-liṅga that has been revealed.
Within this flow of Great Bliss, it is therefore like a distinct stream.
The distinction between Brahmā and Viṣṇu is demonstrated in the *mantraliṅga*;
by Śiva, the Supreme Self, the sequence of difference and non-difference regarding the *prāṇaliṅga* has been shown in the *śivaliṅga*, which consists of six syllables.
Merely by knowing that distinction, one will become liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
Even when there is intense pain from the so-called solar wheel (sūryacakra),
the prāṇaliṅga known as Śivānanda is revealed.
Having conquered the Śaivas, Vaiṣṇavas, Cārvākas, Buddhists, Kṣapaṇakas, and Kaulas through the power of the *prāṇaliṅga*, may there be auspiciousness at the state of Śiva!
The sequence of the *prāṇaliṅga* has been declared; now hear the sequence of the *dalācāra*.
Purity of mind, auspicious conduct, worship of Śiva at the three junctions of the day,
the mantra of Śiva, meditation on Śiva, the wearing of the five mudrās,
pilgrimage to sacred sites, and the study of the scriptures of Śiva.
The sacred site of Maheśvara is a wonder that conquers the senses and the mind;
it bestows clarity of mind, gentleness, a longing for the worship of Śiva,
devotion toward the *jaṅgama* (living) forms [of the deity], and freedom from desire and anger.
O Maheśvarī, this is called the "petal of grace" in Vīraśaiva.
In Nāda is the immovable liṅga, while the bindu is the moving [liṅga];
the supreme moving place is that which is joined with both Nāda and Bindu.
To devotees, he is the form of compassion; to ascetics, he is the form of forgiveness;
and both of these, O Maheśvarī, are of one and the same form—his dark-blue form.
Thus, if one does not practice by following the sequence of the path as a place of refuge through the state of oneness with all beings, there will be repeated rebirth in the lower realms.
They say that "the state of the unity of the *liṅga*" is the defining characteristic of these six states.
[Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Secret of the Vīrāgama," in the Sahasrakoṭi-saṃhitā of the Śrī Vīraśaiva Āgama. Salutations to Śiva! Salutations to Śiva! Salutations to Śiva!
The Secret of the Partless Prāṇaliṅga.
The Mūlādhāra is the station of Brahmā; the Svādhiṣṭhāna belongs to Viṣṇu;
the region of Maṇipūra is that of Rudra; the Anāhata is Maheśvara;
the Viśuddhi is the pure Sādākhya; and the Ājñā-cakra is free from all affliction.
Beyond that, O Goddess, the wise know the supreme station of the Prāṇaliṅga.
Supreme knowledge is in the Ādhāra; the stainless [state] is in the Maṇipūra.
In the Unstruck (anāhata), the supreme bliss (parānanda) is revealed as the vital-force linga (prāṇaliṅga);
in the Pure (viśuddha), the consciousness-constituted linga (cinmayaliṅga) is established; and in the Command (ājñā), it resides in the garland (mālā).
Knowledge pervading all limbs is revealed as the *prāṇaliṅga*;
it is the *tāraka*, the form of devotion, and the *nāda* in its mobile form. O beloved, this form of mine is conjoined with the *tāra-nāda*.
That which does not end in sound is the form of Śiva, while sound consists of Śakti.
The *prāṇaliṅga* is declared to be joined with the beginning and end of the *nāda*.
The letter *A* belongs to Hara, the letter *U* to the one whose vehicle is Garuḍa (Viṣṇu), and the letter *M* has the form of Rudra; thus the triple-formed [Liṅga] becomes mobile.
The topknot, the sacred thread, matted hair, ashes, the carrying of a staff and a water-pot,
the seat, meditation, and the dwelling— these are the characteristics of the mobile [ascetic]. Being the face, the form, and the mantra, one is free from intoxication and delusion.
The illusory body has no impurity; this is the characteristic of the moving [body].
The letter *ja* is the swan-vehicled [Brahmā], the letter *ga* is the one whose banner is Garuḍa [Viṣṇu], and the letter *ma* is the form of Rudra; thus the triple-form becomes mobile.
The syllable *ja* is the form of the Vedas, the syllable *ga* is the Śiva-āgama, and the syllable *ma* is the form of knowledge; therefore, it is called *jaṅgama*.

The letter *ga* is said to be the creator of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), while the letter *ka* is maintenance (*sthiti*). The letter *ma* is indeed withdrawal (*saṃhṛti*), but that which transcends the triad is the moving (*jaṅgama*) reality.
Through anger Rudra came into being, and through affection the Lotus-seated One.
Viṣṇu is the origin through the intellect for all moving embodied beings;
the letter *ja* signifies birth, which does not exist [in Him]; the letter *ga* signifies going, which does not exist [in Him];
the letter *ma* signifies death, which does not exist—this is the characteristic of the Moving One (*jaṅgama*).
Within the Liṅga are the four Vedas; within the Liṅga is the Śiva-āgama;
within the Liṅga are the Siddhas; and within the Liṅga is the Śāmbhava [reality].
Within the Liṅga is the entire universe, the three worlds with all things moving and stationary.
There is nothing superior to that which is external to the *liṅga*; therefore, the *liṅga* is indeed worthy of worship.
Eternal perfection resides at the tip of the fingernails, while liberation is established at the tip of the crest-lock (*śikhā*).
One should worship Śiva as the state of equilibrium between the crest-lock and the two nails.
O fair-faced one, if the tongue conceals its activity, then the entire world is deluded by men,
and my own form is revealed.
A certain teacher may be deficient in feet, while the disciple is deficient in head;
the teacher may be of evil conduct, while the disciple has fallen from his station.
Having learned this from the mouth of the Guru, the *prāṇaliṅga* is revealed:
the reflection of the face in an empty vessel, the fire that fills it, and the unbearable [heat];
the arrow within the heated lac, and the peak of the abode of the melting snow.
O Goddess, if it is the sun, that should be known as the prāṇaliṅga, which is equal to that.
A lotus born from the mud does not, moreover, touch the mud; milk produced from flesh does not, indeed, return to the flesh;
and fire arising from trees does not, again, settle within the tree.
Having learned this from the mouth of the Guru, one should worship the *prāṇaliṅga*.
[Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Niṣkala Prāṇaliṅga," in the *Sahasrakoṭisaṃhitā* of the *Śrīvīraśaivāgama*. Salutations to Śiva.
Salutation to Śiva. Salutation to Śiva.
The Rule for the Marks of Knowledge.
O Goddess of the gods, the wise man who worships the *prāṇaliṅga* excels the auspicious Lord Paśupati of the Great Vow (*mahāvrata*) and the Kāmamukha [deity].
The worshippers of the Jñānatantra, Yogatantra, and Śaivatantra,
having conquered [the world] through the worship of the prāṇaliṅga, went to the city of Śiva.
O beloved, among the acts of knowledge, charity, austerity, pilgrimage, recitation, and self-study, this indeed is the supreme dharma: the worship of the *liṅga* of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Worship beyond the vital-organ liṅga, austerity beyond the vital-organ liṅga,
and knowledge beyond the vital-organ liṅga are difficult to find in all those worlds.
Omniscience is established, as are the purifications of the powers such as *aṇimā*;
these are attained by those who possess the vital breath as their sign (*prāṇaliṅgin*), but they do not exist for others.
Victory over the three worlds, the capacity to sustain the three worlds,
and the performance of the five-fold cosmic functions within the three worlds are accomplished for those who possess the *prāṇaliṅga*.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—
all these great-souled ones are devoted solely to the Prāṇaliṅga.
The Sun, the Moon, Skanda, the lords of the gods and other deities,
the sages, Siddhas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and the Kinnara tribes—
all these attained their status through the worship of the Prāṇaliṅga and by means of the primordial mantras.
The universe is declared to be *prāṇa*, and the universal self (*viśvātmā*) is called the *liṅga*;
the essential reality (*tattva*) of the perfect fusion of these two is proclaimed as the *prāṇaliṅga*.
This entire universe is the Śaktipīṭha; it is called Śiva, the soul of the universe.
This very Śiva, conjoined with the universe, is the Prāṇaliṅga.
That which is visible is the Śaktipīṭha, while that which is invisible is called Śiva;
the Prāṇaliṅga is declared to be within both the visible and the invisible.
The individual soul (jīvātman) is the seat of power (śaktipīṭha), while that which is invisible is called Śiva;
the inner essence of both the visible and the invisible is declared to be the vital-organ (prāṇaliṅga).
The individual soul (jīvātman) is the seat of power (śaktipīṭha), while the supreme soul (paramātman) is the liṅga;
O Goddess, the harmonious union of these two is declared to be the prāṇaliṅga.
This is declared to be the seat of mantra (mantrapīṭha); the meaning of the mantra is called the liṅga.
O sirs, through the realization of both the mantra and its meaning, they speak of the prāṇaliṅga.
They know the seat of power (śaktipīṭha) to be beyond action, characterized by the liṅga of the Self.
The state of their essential identity (samarasa) is to be known as the *prāṇaliṅga* proclaimed by Śiva;
the heart is the seat of power (*śaktipīṭha*), and the self (*ātman*) is indeed called the *liṅga*.
The state of their equilibrium is to be known as the *prāṇaliṅga* declared by Śiva.
The heart is the seat of power (*śaktipīṭha*), wherein the *prāṇaliṅga* resides. When these two—the attained seat and the *liṅga*—reach dissolution, that is their merging.
Likewise, for anyone who breaks the life-force-liṅga (prāṇaliṅga), the guru is the liṅga, devotion is the pedestal, and one's own merit is the flower; thus, praise is the ritual act.
The measure is fragrance and water; the supreme offering is the accomplishment (siddhi).
The three worlds constitute the seat of power (śaktipīṭha); the light-linga (jyotirliṅga) is blissful, and the mantra is the person (manu).
Without action, there is indeed the accomplishment of rite; his worship is performed through meditative absorption (samādhi).
By the cessation of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, the foundation of the oyster-shell [of the heart] is produced.
This is declared to be the definition of the prāṇaliṅga.
They say the individual soul (jīvātman) is the pedestal (pīṭha), while the Supreme Soul (paramātman) alone is the linga.
This is declared to be the "liṅga of the vital breath" (prāṇaliṅga) and is determined in the Śiva scriptures.
[It is characterized by] smearing ashes on all limbs and wearing matted hair and saffron robes.
One who recites the five-syllable mantra a hundred times, who is peaceful, has conquered the mind,
is free from desire, devoted to the guru, and is beyond shame and worldly activity.
And for ascetics dwelling in a secluded place, there is freedom from fear.
Having recognized him as one who knows the meaning of all scriptures and is expert in the knowledge of reality,
the Guru explained to him the characteristics of the Prāṇaliṅga,
as well as how the Liṅgas of origin and the mantras that bestow spiritual perfection arise.
The instruction should be understood from the mouth of the true guru exactly as it is.
Austerity is the body, the Śaktipīṭha; its soul is the supreme Śiva.
Together with the vital breath (prāṇa), he is the possessor of the mark (liṅgin); that mark is the Prāṇaliṅga.
The six paths are said to be the six-petalled [lotus], and that which pervades it is called the *liṅga*.
Śiva is the pervasive one who pervades the six paths and the qualities;
the Śiva-yogins call this very thing the *prāṇaliṅga*.
For whosoever possesses an equal-mindedness toward both, [he is liberated].
For him alone does the knowledge of Śiva shine forth as the *prāṇaliṅga*.
Śiva is the heart of Prāṇa; Prāṇa is the heart of Śiva.
The Lord effects the union of Śiva and the Praṇava.
He alone is the moving embodiment of merit; he is the devotee of the Supreme Self;
he is all-knowing and a knower of all times; he is ascetic and the awakener of truth.
Those who always remember Śiva— who consists of all-knowledge, who is filled with indivisible bliss, and who resembles ten million fires of cosmic destruction— [attain liberation].
The wise person should meditate in their mind upon the Lord, who resembles ten million moons, who dwells within the lunar disc, and who has the moon as his crest-ornament.
Upon the seat consisting of the bliss of Brahman, in the ocean of the essence of the bliss of Brahman,
one should worship Śiva, who is the bliss of Brahman and is attached to the essence of the bliss of Brahman.
Having meditated properly upon Sadāśiva during the morning, midday, and evening worship services at their respective times, one should worship with supreme joy.
In this manner and so forth, one should worship Śiva at the three times of day;
having recited the five-syllabled *haṃsa*, perform the worship of the *prāṇaliṅga*.
Having worshipped in this sequence, the gods, the asuras, and the sages attain liberation; I speak the truth, the absolute truth.
[Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Jñānaliṅga," in the Sahasrakoṭi-saṃhitā of the Śrīvīraśaivāgama. Salutations to Śiva.
Having meditated upon Mahādeva (Vaṃ) in the mūlacakra, there shall be the petal of devotion.
In the Brahma-cakra, the great liṅga is the petal of Maheśvara;
in the Viṣṇu-cakra, the great liṅga is declared to be the petal of Prasāda.
In the Rudra-cakra is the great liṅga, which is the petal of the vital-force liṅga (prāṇaliṅga);
in the Śiva-cakra is the great bliss, the supreme petal of the unity of the liṅgas.
Thus, the characteristics of the six-petaled worship have been described:
mantra-worship is the petal of devotion, meditation-worship belongs to Maheśvara,
yoga-worship is called grace (prasāda), and by means of the self, it is the *prāṇaliṅga*.
O Dear One, worship through meditative absorption (samādhi) constitutes the worship of the feet, while knowledge constitutes the worship of the linga;
thus they say, such is the sixfold characteristic.

O auspicious one, tell me how people should grasp Śiva, who transcends the universe, who is Sadāśiva in the form of the Liṅga, and whose conduct consists of the Guṇas; likewise, O Lord, how is the worship of the Liṅga performed, and how is it concluded?
How are the offerings of flowers presented, and what are the sixteen modes of service?
By means of which actions of mind, speech, and body does one reach Śiva, who is far, far beyond?
By whom has His Liṅga been seen, and by whom, moreover, has the sequence of worship been realized?
How can there be action for Maheśa, whose nature is partless bliss?
In the world of mortals, they declare that which is free from the division of the Guru to be [the Self],
wherein mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṃkāra), consciousness (citta), and the five senses do not arise.
O Ambikā, how [should one know] Maheśvara, Śambhu, the Supreme Self?
Because it is visible, that which is left over by a dog is impure; because of its memory, that which is left over by a crow becomes defiled.
The entire world is the leavings of the elements (bhūtas), while that which arises from mantras is the leavings of the individual soul (jīva).
Water is the leavings of a fish, and a flower is the leavings of a bee.
Because incense and lamps are displayed, there may likewise be some residue from the fire-offering.
All the worlds remain beneath the Liṅga like a sesame seed;
within all of them, living beings do not possess even the size of an atom.
O man, among those deities such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others, where is there even a trace of atomicity?
How can a stone not deserve to be weighed, and how does it assume the form of a *liṅga*? And how does the worship of that *liṅga* become the worship of Śiva?
This may cause delusion among those who do not understand it:
that there is no pedestal for the *liṅga*, nor any end to this *liṅga*;
that everything consists of the *liṅga*, and that perfection and prosperity arise from the supreme *liṅga*.
By whom has that which is to be seen and known been perceived—the moving and the unmoving situated within the subtle body?
O Goddess, you alone are that *liṅga*; indeed, the *liṅga* is the state of consciousness itself.
Being devoid of the seen, the unseen, and so forth, there is no reality [beyond it]; how then can there be ritual action?
Indeed, the worlds are like waves in the nectar-ocean of Śivānanda;
he who has established the waters of the shoreless ocean as both the graspable and the shore itself.
O Supreme Goddess, such indeed are the teacher and the disciple,
as well as the worshipped and the worshippers, the grace, and the recipient of that grace.
Pure flowers, faded garlands, pure water, and a composed mind—incense, lamps, and ointment: all of this is mere mockery.
Śambhu consists of the offering, and He is the bestower of the fruit of the offering;
with the realization that "the Great Lord is both the giver and the enjoyer," one should indeed know that everything has become identical with Śiva, and nothing other than Śiva is seen.
One should not conceive of existence in two ways; for such a person, knowledge does not exist.
He in whose mind the doctrine of non-dual knowledge (*abheda-jñāna*) operates is a Guru; he is Śiva, meritorious, omniscient, and a knower of all the Vedas.
He is a knower of reality, an initiated one, a perfected being (*siddha*), a devotee, and a worshiper of Śiva.
Having attained the state of universal bliss through the vision of the Supreme Self,
that Great Soul exists among the Śaivas, Vīraśaivas, Vaidikas, and those of mixed traditions; yet in the world of mortals, he is not bound by fetters, nor by the Tantras.
He is initiated through the initiation of knowledge, firmly established in the state of Śambhu.
Having thus learned the worship of Śiva from the mouth of the Guru, O beloved of the Guru,
[one realizes that] due to ignorance and lack of scriptural knowledge, bondage by the fetters occurs as if following a non-path.
Having understood the sequence according to the scriptures, there is liberation from the bondage of the fetters.
The acquisition of bondage through fetters brings suffering, whereas the release from those fetters bestows happiness.
The noose is the threefold impurity; from its increase, birth proceeds.
The wise constantly proceed from that state beyond impurity to the plane of Śiva.
Hope is said to be a bond; freedom from hope is the release from the bond.
This very thing, which is devoid of hope and despair, is the mark of the vital breath (prāṇaliṅga);
the mental activity that causes birth is bondage, while the turning back of the mind is liberation.
Cessation and engagement, the internal mark of those two,
as well as the birth and death of men— of these, the cause is found right here.
Their distinction and their state of equilibrium, however, are the stable [state] of the mind of the Mother.
Having certainly taken up the path of the auspicious convention belonging to you alone.

[Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Guru and Disciple together with the Characteristics of the Petals of the Six Chakras," in the *Sahasrakoṭisaṃhitā* of the *Śrīvīraśaivāgama*.]
O Śaṅkara, what is the fruit for those who know the Vedas by merely wearing matted hair? I wish to know [the fruit] of both mobile and immobile liṅgas.
Īśvara said:
Oh, what great fortune! What supreme fortune is this—the wearing of matted hair and rudrākṣas!
Matted hair, sacred ash, rudrākṣas, and the worship of the Śiva-liṅga constitute [this path].
Those Rudras, who are the very embodiments of Rudra, shine resplendent throughout the three worlds.
