They bear the Śiva-liṅga, the rudrākṣa, the smearing of sacred ash (vibhūti),
matted hair, the sacrificial thread, a loincloth, and a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).
A staff, sandals, earrings, and a yogic belt.
In his mouth, he held the five-syllable mantra, being entirely devoted to the yoga of meditation.
He was dispassionate and free from attachment, avoiding the censure of others;
he had completely renounced association with worldly existence and avoided worldly conversation; he was devoted to the worship of the Śiva-liṅga and desired to go on pilgrimages to sacred fords.
Devoid of middle meat and the like, it is offered at the three times by one possessing knowledge.
Thus all the sages joyfully declare that Śaṅkara, who is distinguished by such qualities, is the supreme Lord in embodied form, yet not different from the Absolute.
All the deities declare that he who performs the worship of the *prāṇaliṅga* and wears matted hair and rudrākṣa beads is indeed the supreme Śiva himself.
By wearing matted hair, rudrākṣas, and the liṅga, they become practitioners whose very life-force is the liṅga (prāṇaliṅgin).
For those meritorious men, there is no fear of merit or sin. Whether a householder, one who is dispassionate, or one free from worldly desire, provided he is endowed with affection [for his kin].
For this wearer of the *prāṇaliṅga*, there is indeed no fear of merit or sin;
even a courtesan’s husband, a thief, or one who has consorted with another’s wife [is freed].
If someone becomes a bearer of the *prāṇaliṅga*, no fault is found in him.
Whether she be a woman of noble family, a courtesan, a maidservant, a widow, or one in her menses— even a woman of the *caṇḍāla* caste— there are many such women upon the earth.
From their union, no fault arises, just as there is none from the offering of the vital breath into the liṅga.
Matted hair, a rosary of rudrākṣa beads, sacred ash, and the worship of Śiva.
Sin shall not touch a person who is intent on the recitation of the five-syllable mantra.
Whether he be most wicked, of evil conduct, a sinner, or even one guilty of a secondary offense.
By beholding the matted locks, the sacred ash, and the worship, one is liberated from all evil.
If one who is devoted to the worship of Śiva with matted hair perceives [Śiva] as abiding within the nature of the Śivaliṅga,
no fault is found in him even if he is possessed of great sins.
The three impurities, the three qualities, the defects, the destroyer of vows, and the sin against Brahman.
A person who wears matted hair is meritorious; through the worship of Śiva, he destroys all [evil].
On the body of this meritorious wearer of matted hair, there are clusters of body hair.
O Umā, here the Vedas, Śāstras, and Āgamas declare that the very *liṅgas* are born from their limbs; they are pervasive and yet subject to cutting.
One must not perform the cutting of the *vṛtti* (the stalk/base) as prescribed by the Śruti, for if one does so, it constitutes the breaking of the *liṅga*.
Shaving, cutting, and plucking out the hair of those who bear the marks of life [the vital organs] are [prohibited].

It must never be done; if one were to do so, it would result in the loss of the *liṅga*. O Dear One, wherever that *prāṇaliṅga*—composed of consciousness—resides, whether in the bodies of living beings, in their hearts, or in their hands, [it is there].
Remaining there, O Goddess of Gods, I tell you the truth, the absolute truth:
when the vital breaths have dissolved into the Samāna, it causes one to depart.
It is proclaimed as the "liṅga of breath" (prāṇaliṅga); therefore, it is that very prāṇaliṅga.
Among other types of liṅgas, no such status as an assistant is found.
Therefore, all [should seek] the fruit of worship, not greed; such are ordinary people.
Just as the vital breath (prāṇa) is, so is the liṅga; just as the wind pervades the *haṃsa*, for this very reason the wise know it as the *prāṇaliṅga*.
The *liṅga* mixed with *prāṇa*, and *prāṇa* mixed with the *liṅga*—
through the knowledge of the union of these two, it is called *prāṇaliṅga*.
Human beings and all other living creatures are bound by the three impurities;
the gods are bound by two impurities; and Brahmā and Viṣṇu are bound by one.
Neither among the gods nor among humans does my wealth exist;
for men who possess the liṅga of the vital breath, no bondage of impurity exists.
The Śrī Devī said:
How could Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the lords of the gods be bound by impurity?
For how is it that they are not bound by impurity merely by wearing the liṅga?
Īśvara said:
Whoever on the surface of the earth has been initiated into the Vīra-tantras,
in him the Lord Śiva, the Supreme Self, dwells.
Therefore, when a man is freed from impurities and bears the *prāṇaliṅga*,
even ants flee at the mere proximity of the fire.
By the mere presence of Śiva, all impurities flee elsewhere.
Having assumed the Prāṇaliṅga, Maheśvara himself has made this scripture;
this is the truth, and I have sworn it thrice.
The Goddess said:
"O Supreme Lord, tell me what the three qualities— rajas, tamas, and sattva— do for bodies."
I do not know its distinctions in detail, exactly as they are.
Īśvara said:
"O Mahādeva, by means of the three qualities (guṇas), human beings are born; by the quality of passion (rājasa), [they become] Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas."
Hari is manifest through the *sāttvika* [nature], and Śiva through the *nirguṇa* immortals;
yet among all my devotees, those who bear the *prāṇaliṅga* are superior.
The Nigamas and Āgamas declare that there is an absence of the three qualities (guṇas) in them.
The paternal property belongs to the sons according to the established rules of ritual action;
however, as for me, who have transcended the three qualities (guṇas), it does not belong to them.
In the Vīra-tantras, the fault of initiation and consecration is destroyed;
I am that Vīramāheśvara, and O Umā, my devotees are equal to me.
Therefore, all the gods and asuras worship that which has the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as its emblem.
This supreme secret of Vīraśaivism has been revealed;
by my grace, O Hero, they do not know that it resides within you.
O Maheśvarī, he is beyond qualities, beyond impurities, and beyond karma;
he is the person who has transcended the mind, possesses great bliss, and bears the *liṅga* of vital breath.
[Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Greatness of the Specific Darśana," in the *Sahasrakoṭisaṃhitā* of the *Śrīvīraśaivāgama*.]
The Śrī Devī said:
What is the origin of *vibhūti*, and what is this fruit of *vibhūti*?
In what place on the body is *vibhūti* to be worn, and what is its characteristic mark?
"I wish to hear all of that; tell it to me in detail.
The Lord said: "Well asked by you, O Goddess! The manifestation of power (*vibhūti*) is the cause of origination."
The fourfold manifestation has been proclaimed; however, the first is described in certain places.
O Great Goddess, the form of fire arises within my body;
it is seen as the fiery ash of the worlds, O Pārvatī.
The connection of fire with ash,
and the connection of ash with fire, is proclaimed as a relationship of inseparable concomitance (avinābhāva) based on the ash.
Indeed, among gods, asuras, and humans, they do not know that which is born of ashes;
through purity one is born from ashes, for in that state there is no attachment.

From the stainless [state], consciousness arises as light; from that light, the sky of consciousness is born. From the sky of consciousness, sound (nāda) arises, and from sound, the point (bindu) is produced.
From the point and sound comes the Supreme Power (parāśakti), and from the Supreme Power, Sadāśiva.
From Maheśa comes Sadāśivā, and from Maheśa comes the Lord Hara.
Therefore, from Viṣṇu the four-faced Brahmā was produced,
and from the four-faced one came the three worlds, this universe consisting of the five elements.
Earth is the form of Brahmā, and Janārdana is the form of water.
Mahādeva is the form of fire; Maheśvara is the form of wind;
Sadāśiva is the form of space—these are their characteristics in order.

The cremation ground of Śambhu is proclaimed to be the end of the Yugas; some say that I am he who is smeared with its ashes. Because it is the destruction of the senses, it is called "peace" (*śānti*) and "ashes" (*bhasma*).
Some say that because of the burning of Kāma, he became ashes;
all of that was spoken by each of his mouths repeatedly according to their own will.
O Maheśānī, I shall now describe to you that which remains of him.
O Great Goddess, the form of Agni arises together with Āgneyī; he is the self-born and the manifestation, and manifestation is the cause of all.
Birth occurs through manifestation as the element, and birth occurs within manifestation, O Hara.

Through his power (vibhūti) comes the birth of Rudra; Maheśvara resides within that power. Through his power arises Sadāśiva; they say his coming and going are eternal. Through his power exist all the gods, and through his power exists all that is moving and unmoving.
By his power he is the cosmic eggs; by his power the seven oceans;
by his power he is the form of dissolution; by his power he is the cause of creation.
Furthermore, for all others there is rebirth, but never for the ash.
By the mere application of ash, there is no rebirth at all—
for any living beings or deities, O Umā.

Furthermore, for the ashes, there is neither rebirth nor death; yet everything exists within them. Because of their stainlessness, the ashes are said to be stainless and pure, and they are considered pure throughout the three worlds.
And because of their stainlessness among the elements, they are to be worshipped by gods and asuras alike.
O God, by wearing the *vibhūti*, the wise attain the state of Śiva;
first, listen to how the bodies of Śiva were covered with falling ashes.
Therefore, O Goddess of the Suras, a certain udumbara tree born from those grains quickly bowed down in wonder.
Its length and breadth were eighty million *lakṣakoṭis*,
and its height was of that same measure from root to the very top;
it was perpetually filled with fruits upon its many branches.

On that tree there is a single fruit; within that fruit are millions of worms, and those very worms are seen as the fourteen worlds. In this same way, O Ambika, this world is indeed [the product of] Māyā.
And among these, all the gods indeed have their heads held in pride;
Nārāyaṇa is remembered as the one who can bring about the destruction of the power of all the gods.
Vibhūti is all the gods, and Maheśvara is Vibhūti;
O Goddess, Sadāśiva is traditionally known as Vibhūti at all times.
[The merit comes] from seeing, touching, wearing, and repeatedly sprinkling [it].
For those people who dwell in Vāraṇasī until the end of the kalpa, [the merit] is equal to thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of vājapeya sacrifices.
The killing of a Brahmin, the killing of a cow, and whatever other sins one may have—
including violating the teacher’s bed, drinking liquor, the murder of a woman, and the destruction of the linga—
all great sins (mahāpāpa) and minor sins (upapāpa) are destroyed by the wearing of this sacred ash.
There are thirty-five million sacred sites in the three worlds;
by merely bathing in the *vibhūti*, one certainly obtains their fruit.

At the time of sacrifice, at the time of austerity, at the time of worship, as well as during silent recitation (japa), in giving, in fire-offerings (homa), and in the meditation on Śiva, the wise man should perform the bath with sacred ash. Without the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), the ancestral rite (śrāddha) is incomplete; without the triple mark, the oblation (huta) is incomplete.
A gift given without the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is proclaimed to be demonic.
The entire accumulation of sins committed over thousands of future births perishes in an instant for men through the touch of sacred ash (vibhūti).

Even if a man stands firm on one leg for ten million hundred years, he is not worth even a sixteenth part of the merit of bathing in sacred ash (vibhūti). One should [wear] sacred ash, the Śiva-linga, and a rosary for the recitation of the Rudrākṣa mantra.
This bowing is always performed by reciting [the name] behind one's back;
O Goddess, by wearing sacred ashes (vibhūti), even another person may become a twice-born (dvija).
Without sacred ashes, even a knower of the four Vedas becomes a Caṇḍāla—such is the Smṛti.

An enemy of the guru, an enemy of Śiva, a sinner, or one guilty of minor offenses—by the mere wearing of sacred ash (bhūti), he becomes Rudra himself; of this there is no doubt. Even a drinker of liquor, a killer of an embryo, a wicked soul, or one who violates the teacher’s bed [is purified].

Merely by bathing with the *vibhūti*, the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those of mixed castes attained the state of having their sins destroyed. For all these castes, the wearing of the *puṇḍra* must be performed.
Whether one is a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or a mendicant,
the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) must be performed as the cause for attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The triple mark (tripuṇḍra), the half-mark (ardhapuṇḍra), the circular mark, the crescent moon,
the lamp-shaped mark, and the linga— these six are the marks of Śiva.
Vināyaka, the householder star, and whatever other minor beings there may be [are likewise associated with these].
Upon seeing the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), they flee; of this there is no doubt.
Having committed theft and having committed adultery with another's wife,
having drunk liquor and having committed the murder of a Brahmin—
one who bathes in ashes and lies upon a bed of ashes [is purified].
One who meditates upon Rudra is liberated from all sins.
Corrupted by heresy, people will practice the smearing with ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) only according to a path taught in the Vedas;
yet [true] ash is the bringer of prosperity, incomparable purity, and the destroyer of the flood of sins.

The destroyer of all calamities, the great increaser of good fortune, the protector against spirits, ghosts, piśācas, rākṣasas, planetary influences, and portents of misfortune— this Bhūti, which directly bestows the fruit of liberation, has been revealed; let it always be worn.
It is prosperity, bringing prosperity to men; it is protection, the supreme protector.
It is called *bhasita* because it destroys worldly existence (*bhava*), and *bhasma* because it scorns (*bharlsana*) all impurity (*kalmaṣa*).
"There is no doubt that the name 'Śiva' is indeed ashes and light";
thus the Jābāla Upaniṣad declares all this with supreme joy.
Whatever merit is found in all sacred fords and whatever fruit is obtained from all sacrifices—that fruit is multiplied ten millionfold by the ash-bath; of this there is no doubt.
The merit of bathing with ashes is countless times greater than that of bathing with water;
therefore, setting aside other forms of bathing, one should perform the fiery bath (āgneyasnāna).
One should apply the consecrated ashes while reciting the mantra "Mā nas toke."
The Tripuṇḍra mark made with ashes on the middle finger, the ring finger,
and the thumb is auspicious and destructive of great sins.
The Ūrdhvapuṇḍra belongs to the Sāma Veda, and the Madhyapuṇḍra to the Yajur Veda.
The lower *puṇḍra* is the *Ṛgveda* itself; therefore, the *puṇḍra* is called *triyāyuṣa*.
On the forehead, at the two armpits, in the middle of the two [shoulders], and at the two wrists.
In the region of the navel, the abdomen, as well as in the heart and the throat;
A wise person should wear sacred ash on the two sides, at the roots of the ears, on the two parts of the back, and likewise on the head, during the three junctions of the day.
In bathing, giving gifts, performing *śrāddha*, the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, and the worship of the gods,
one who has applied the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) becomes a purified soul and conquers death.
One who applies a sectarian mark (puṇḍra) with only one hand or applies it facing downwards shall pass through a hundred births as a dog and then go to the Raurava hell.
The *puṇḍra* should be two cubits in length; one should apply it facing upwards.
By this, O Goddess, one is liberated and attains union with Śiva (*śivasāyujya*).
If someone were to unknowingly pour water onto ashes at night somewhere;
One shall go to the Raurava hell for as many years as there are particles of dust [on the ground],
whether one does so while impure from food remnants, in a cremation ground, during a birth-impurity, or even at a death-impurity.

One should not touch ashes at the time of chewing betel, during sexual intercourse, or while joking; should anyone touch them at such times, they shall go to hell. Likewise, having touched fish or meat, or having urinated in the forest, [one must purify oneself].
O Goddess, no one should touch ashes during an impure weeping.
Pure, ascetic, well-minded, pleasant-faced, speaking the truth,
and endowed with faith in the afterlife— one shall constantly attain prosperity.
That devotee, initiated by Śiva, attains union with Śiva (śivasāyujya).
However, ashes from a potter’s workshop, from a place where bricks are burnt,
or from within a kitchen (māhāsya/mahānasa) must not be collected.
The ash of the Agnihotra sacrifice, and that ash which is in the presence of Śiva—that ash leads to union with Śiva; one should not touch any other ash.
A Caṇḍāla, a slanderer, a drinker of intoxicants, a physician,
one afflicted with skin diseases, a cripple, a liar, a sower of discord,
one deficient in limbs, one of evil conduct, and one who has committed the five great sins.
Or he may indicate this, or indeed show it to Śivā.
One should avoid ash that is smoky-colored or red;
one should wear pure ash and discard everything else.
The black [variety] is said to cause disease and shall be a destroyer of one's reputation.
Smoky-colored [mercury] causes the destruction of life when drunk, and yellow [mercury] brings about the ruin of prosperity;
white [mercury] results in the attainment of all perfections—this is the certainty established by the Vedānta.
